newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore says no China policy change on fund raising.
newsitem.headline: Gore says no China policy change on fund raising.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore has told China there would be no immediate change in U.S. policy following allegations that Beijing made illegal payments to the U.S. Democratic party, a senior official said on Wednesday.
However, Gore stressed that the United States would regard the matter very seriously if the charges were proved.
"It is premature to say that an investigation that hasn't been completed yet is going to have a major impact on the relationship," said the senior U.S. official who declined to be identified.

"If the allegations are later proven to be true then they are very serious and we'll deal with it at that time," said the official who took part in talks on Tuesday between Gore and Chinese Premier Li Peng.
"The controversy by itself without facts being established does not have an impact on the relationship, and should not," he said.

China's Li had raised the scandal in Tuesday's meeting with Gore and "vigorously denied" that Beijing had sent funds into campaign coffers of Democratic Party candidates in the 1996 elections, the official said.
The official said Gore, in his talks with Li, "told him we considered the allegations very serious".

But Gore told the Chinese leader "that what was important to us is not the discussion of this controversy. The controversy is of no consequence if the allegations turn out to be untrue. If they are true, then that is another matter."

The high-ranking U.S. official was seeking to qualify comments by another official, who late on Tuesday stressed that Gore used the meeting to reassure China there would be no change in the U.S. policy of engagement because of the controversy.
China's Li had responded by saying he was reassured this would not affect Washington's pledges to improve ties with Beijing, the official said on Tuesday.
However, the official on Wednesday stressed that Gore "explicitly said that we take this very seriously and if the allegations are true, yes it will be a serious matter".

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign funds from foreign corporations.
The fundraising uproar is particularly sensitive for Gore, because he and U.S. President Bill Clinton have been accused of questionable fund raising practices in their re-election campaign.

The Democratic Party was forced to say it was refunding some $3 million in contributions after an investigation suggested the money may have come from illegal sources, many from various interests in Asia.

Gore launched his first full day in China as the most senior official to visit Beijing since the 1989 crackdown on student demonstrations with a series of high-level talks and is scheduled to meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday.
Members of the U.S. delegation said little had been done to bridge the gap between the two countries on human rights but talks on the issue were less acrimonious than in the past.
Gore and Li presided over signings of two multi-million dollar contracts for U.S. business in China, signalling a thaw in once chilly ties between Beijing and Washington.
